note: Three axes: technical domain x role function x organizational context. Job titles are aliases for combinations, and none of the axes produces a ranking. This file is where changes are made. The eight axes, two scales and four levels use the same values as the Mechanical Engineering Core: results from two majors can only be compared on the same ruler, and building a new ruler for each major would break comparison within a university

J1.name: Problem definition
J1.question: Who decided what to work on?

J2.name: Requirements interpretation
J2.question: Did you turn the requirements into numbers and constraints?

J3.name: Technical decisions
J3.question: Which items did you decide yourself?

J4.name: Methods and tools
J4.question: What did you use, and how?

J6.name: Comparison and verification
J6.question: What did you compare it against?

J7.name: Failure and correction
J7.question: How did you narrow down what went wrong?

J8.name: Organizational use
J8.question: Who used it, and for what?

S4.note: Screening scale. The four axes asked at BASIC. Organizational use is left out of screening because it puts undergraduates at a structural disadvantage: whether your work was used by an organization can only be answered if you were placed in one, and someone who has only done classes and a capstone will have that cell empty even if they made decisions. Organizational use is asked only in the in-depth stage

S8.note: Full scale. STANDARD and above. Do not use S8 as the denominator for S4. What the in-depth stage newly opens are the four axes not in screening (problem definition, requirements interpretation, methods and tools, organizational use)

levels.L1: Exposed. Watched or reused what someone else did
levels.L3: Owned. Decided it myself, and the result was used

technical_domains.name: Software Design and Architecture
technical_domains.owns: Settles what to build, the module boundaries and the interfaces

technical_domains.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
technical_domains.owns: Settles how data is represented and the limits of computational complexity

technical_domains.name: Server and API Development
technical_domains.owns: Settles the flow for receiving and processing requests and the response contract

technical_domains.name: Data Storage and Query Design
technical_domains.owns: Settles how data is stored and the paths used to find it

technical_domains.name: User Interface Development
technical_domains.owns: Settles the screen's state structure, input handling and accessibility

technical_domains.name: Systems and Concurrent Programming
technical_domains.owns: Settles memory and concurrency policy within one machine

technical_domains.name: Networks and Distributed Systems
technical_domains.owns: Settles the communication rules between machines and how partial failures are handled

technical_domains.name: Information Security
technical_domains.owns: Assumes threats and settles what is allowed and where to block

technical_domains.name: Machine Learning and Data Analysis
technical_domains.owns: Settles the patterns to extract from data and the conditions for measuring performance

technical_domains.name: Testing, Quality and Release Operations
technical_domains.owns: Settles pass criteria, deployment procedures and rollback paths

technical_domains.name: Real-Time Graphics and Game Development
technical_domains.owns: Settles the compute budget within one frame and the drawing order

role_functions.name: Design and development
role_functions.success: One buildable option that meets the requirements

role_functions.name: Performance analysis and estimation
role_functions.output_kind: Performance analysis, capacity estimates, complexity reasoning
role_functions.success: Evidence that matches measurements and changed the design

role_functions.name: Testing and verification
role_functions.one_line: Checks that what was built is right
role_functions.success: Results with reproducible verdicts and a stated scope

role_functions.name: Build and deployment automation
role_functions.output_kind: Deployment procedures, environment configuration, rollback paths
role_functions.success: The same input yields the same output, and it can be rolled back

role_functions.name: Service operations
role_functions.output_kind: Operations metrics, incident records, response procedures
role_functions.success: Uptime stays within the commitment and the same outage does not recur

role_functions.name: Integration and coordination
role_functions.one_line: Brings many people's decisions together into one

role_functions.name: Exploration and research
role_functions.one_line: Narrows down questions that do not have answers yet
role_functions.success: The question is narrowed and a method remains

role_functions.name: Quality and reliability
role_functions.one_line: Assures that requirements hold throughout operation
role_functions.success: Defects do not recur and the reasons behind verdicts are traceable

role_functions_note: Eight of them, using the **same codes** as the Mechanical Engineering Core. Role functions are a layer above majors, so they are not rebuilt for each major. Only two names changed: `Process and Mass Production` and `Operation and Maintenance` are manufacturing terms, and software students would not find themselves in them. What each role does is kept word for word, so the axes did not split; what differs is the kind of output produced: design documents, deployment procedures and operations metrics take the place of drawings

org_contexts.name: Product companies running their own services
org_contexts.performance: User metrics, response time, operating cost
org_contexts.differs: You build your own service and run it for years

org_contexts.name: Solution and platform vendors
org_contexts.performance: Meeting customer needs, compatibility, unit price
org_contexts.differs: You build products other companies use and follow agreed rules

org_contexts.name: Contract development and technical services
org_contexts.performance: Deadlines, meeting acceptance conditions, repeat business
org_contexts.differs: You build to customer requirements and hand over by the agreed deadline

org_contexts.name: Government-funded research institutes
org_contexts.performance: Program goals, technology readiness, potential for technology transfer
org_contexts.differs: Work runs on government-funded programs, and interim reviews set the schedule

org_contexts.name: Universities and research labs
org_contexts.differs: You question whether your methods are sound and publish them as papers

org_contexts.name: Public sector, regulation and certification
org_contexts.performance: Judgments of compliance with standards and the evidence behind them
org_contexts.differs: You judge whether things meet standards and keep the evidence on record

org_contexts.name: Startups and small teams
org_contexts.performance: A working service, launched before the money runs out
org_contexts.differs: A few people share many roles and ship fast

boundaries.shared: Both are present when deciding what to build
boundaries.b_difference: Picks what to build first from many people's requirements
boundaries.a_question: Have you decided the direction of dependencies between modules yourself?
boundaries.b_question: Have you sorted out yourself which of the requirements you received would not be accepted?

boundaries.shared: Both write code that runs fast
boundaries.a_difference: Responsible for data representation and computational complexity
boundaries.b_difference: Responsible for the contract for receiving requests and returning responses
boundaries.a_question: Have you changed a data structure to reduce complexity?
boundaries.b_question: Have you set the response contract and error codes yourself?

boundaries.pair: Server development vs. data storage design
boundaries.shared: Both receive requests and handle data
boundaries.a_difference: Responsible for the request handling flow and the response contract
boundaries.b_difference: Responsible for the storage structure and query performance
boundaries.a_question: Have you made a request safe to receive twice?
boundaries.b_question: Have you added an index to cut query time?

boundaries.shared: Both build screens people look at
boundaries.a_difference: Responsible for state changes, input handling and accessibility
boundaries.b_difference: Responsible for the compute budget within one frame and the drawing order
boundaries.a_question: Have you decided yourself where screen state should live?
boundaries.b_question: Have you lowered quality to fit within the frame budget?

boundaries.shared: Both deal with many things running at once
boundaries.a_difference: Responsible for memory and concurrency within one machine
boundaries.b_difference: Responsible for latency and partial failures between machines
boundaries.a_question: Have you set lock scope or memory lifetimes yourself?
boundaries.b_question: Have you set timeout and retry policies yourself?

boundaries.pair: Information security vs. test and verification
boundaries.shared: Both look for conditions that will fail
boundaries.a_difference: Judges by what an attacker could do
boundaries.b_difference: Judges by whether it works as required
boundaries.a_question: Have you assumed a threat and narrowed the allowed access yourself?
boundaries.b_question: Have you set pass criteria and test cases yourself?

boundaries.pair: Machine learning vs. data storage design
boundaries.shared: Both handle large amounts of data
boundaries.a_difference: Extracts patterns from data and evaluates performance
boundaries.b_difference: Decides the structures for storing and finding data
boundaries.a_question: Have you split evaluation conditions to catch overfitting?
boundaries.b_question: Have you set the normalization level and indexes yourself?

boundaries.pair: Machine learning vs. exploration and research
boundaries.a_difference: Brings models to usable performance and hands them over
boundaries.b_difference: Narrows down questions that do not have answers yet
boundaries.a_question: Have you compared against existing methods under the same conditions?
boundaries.b_question: Have you narrowed down a hypothesis you set, through experiments?

boundaries.pair: Testing and deployment vs. service operations
boundaries.shared: Both deal with the path into production
boundaries.a_difference: Builds procedures so the same result repeats
boundaries.a_question: Have you built a rollback path yourself?
boundaries.b_question: Have you set alert thresholds and response steps yourself?

boundaries.b_difference: Blocks what should not get in
boundaries.a_question: Have you narrowed down the causes of latency and loss to a network segment?
boundaries.b_question: Have you written the rules that separate normal traffic from attacks yourself?
